title: What to do before buying a martech platform with AI context
content:
Martech vendors sell context to address gaps in AI agents’ knowledge. But most of what they’re selling is work your team already owns.

Suppose your marketing operations manager types four sentences into the organization’s new campaign agent on Monday morning. By lunch, it’s built a five-email nurture sequence, two landing pages, and a set of paid social ads. Everything launches Wednesday, but the problem doesn’t surface until Friday, when your head of brand notices the third email promises a 60-day money-back guarantee — an offer your company dropped last spring.

Knowledge about the offer was stuck in a legal reviewer’s inbox and in the memory of two people who sat in on a meeting two quarters ago. The agent had never seen the updated information, and nobody had been assigned to check the sequence before it went out.

AI platforms with context can help avoid these problems. But before you invest in one, get clear on your guidelines and approval processes.

title: Nike’s latest marathon campaign is in the pages of the New York Times
content:
Nike’s been known to make a splash around major marathons, even when it’s not an official sponsor.

Following this year’s New York City Marathon, that splash is in ink.

For the first time this year, the New York Times published the full list of marathon finishers in print, an effort that Nike is supporting. The brand sponsored the special sections of the Times on Monday and Tuesday, and it has also been appearing alongside the paper’s digital and newsletter assets, according to Amy Oelkers, SVP of ad sales at New York Times Advertising, who spoke exclusively to Marketing Brew about how the campaign came together.

The campaign falls in line with Nike’s general approach to running sponsorship, which has focused on “moments that mean something to runners,” Seema Simmons, VP and general manager of Nike Running for North America, told us last year.

It’s also indicative of two cultural touchstones that have been of high interest to advertisers, Oelkers said: sports and nostalgia.

Name in lights print

The Times has printed a partial finishers list since 1994, but this year marks the first time the paper included every finisher’s name, which spanned several pages of its Monday and Tuesday national editions. Finishers’ names were broken out by official finish times, with the first half in Monday’s paper and the second half in Tuesday’s. Copies were available in some Nike stores in the city, and runners were able to get them for free at the Times’ online shop.

title: Inside agency efforts to navigate the AEO platform landscape
content:
There’s a plethora of answer engine optimization (AEO) tools on the market. How is an advertiser to make sense of them all?

AEO platforms, which offer tools aimed at boosting brand visibility in AI platforms, are touting various capabilities as they vie for business from brands and agencies. However, as agencies evaluate the tools on the market, factors like a platform’s ability to measure multiple LLMs and its data collection methodology are among the most important in helping a client choose a platform, agency executives told Marketing Brew.

Agencies look at other metrics, like how often the AEO platform refreshes its data, more strategically.

“This is not a lift-and-shift from the success that we’ve had for the last 20+ years in running both paid and organic search programs,” Michael Sondak, Omnicom’s North America SVP, head of search, told Marketing Brew. “It’s wildly different: Different orchestrators, different technology, different dependents, different teams, [and] different talent.”

Choices, choices

With so many AEO platforms on the market, VML isn’t committing to one. Instead, it’s taking into account clients’ marketing mixes and needs to help them choose the right tool for them, Heather Physioc, the agency’s chief discoverability officer, said.

title: How to find and fix your AEO keywords gap
content:
To improve visibility in AI answer engines, content and SEO marketers need to add AEO keywords gap analysis to their strategies. Traditional SEO keyword gaps show which terms a company isn’t ranking for versus the competition. An AEO keywords gap uses the same principle but with broader criteria, identifying the prompts and questions where a given brand is cited in AI search, but another isn’t.

This guide offers a practical pathway to find and close the AEO keywords gap, identifying AI citation opportunities a company is missing. It covers how to audit current content and competitor coverage, how to spot high-value gaps to close first, how to turn gaps into answer-ready content that gets cited, and how to track whether it’s working.

title: Data 360: How We Cut Lead Assignment From 20 Minutes to 20 Seconds
content:
Every year, Salesforce redraws account territories and refreshes its sales routing rules, often just two weeks before they take effect. Under our old process, leads could follow outdated rules for up to six weeks afterward, and sellers fixed misrouted leads by hand. This year, every routing change went live the same day the new policies did.

Getting there meant redesigning our lead routing platform. Assignment happened across three systems, each region had heavily customized rules, and almost every inbound lead went to a sales rep. Live chats and phone calls got fast attention, but everything else landed in one big pile. Someone asking for a demo looked the same as someone who downloaded an article, so reps couldn’t tell serious buyers from casual browsers, and the best leads got lost in the crowd. We were using incomplete data to answer a critical question: is this person ready for a sales conversation?

title: Reaching the Inbox Is the Win. Standing Out Is the Next Challenge.
content:
There is a moment familiar to almost every email marketer.

The campaign is live. Authentication checked out. It didn’t bounce. It didn’t land in spam. Then someone opens Gmail and says, “It’s in Promotions.” Or Yahoo shows it under Offers. Outlook drops it in Other.

Cue the panic: What went wrong? How do we get into Primary next time?

But here’s the thing most marketers miss: the email still reached the inbox.

Promotions, Offers, Newsletters, and Other aren’t the spam folder with better branding. They’re just different rooms inside the same house. Gmail, Yahoo, and Outlook all sort mail this way because they’re trying to help the recipient, not punish the sender. A marketing email landing in Promotions is often just the system recognizing what it is.

That doesn’t mean tab placement is irrelevant. Primary and Focused usually get more immediate attention. But “less immediate” is very different from “not delivered.” Once you’re in the inbox, any part of it, the real question changes. It’s no longer “Did it arrive?” It’s “Will they choose it?”

Delivery, inbox placement, and tab placement are different outcomes

It helps to separate three terms that are often treated as interchangeable.

  • Delivery means the receiving mail server accepted the message. A delivered email may still be routed to spam.
  • Inbox placement means the email reached the recipient’s inbox rather than spam or another filtered destination.

title: Throttling vs. Rate Limiting: Backoff Strategies for Workflows
content:
A burst of 429 (Too Many Requests) errors can bring an otherwise healthy workflow to a halt. Retrying is part of the solution, but timing matters: Retry too quickly and you’re likely to hit the same limit again.

Understanding throttling versus rate limiting helps you respond more intelligently, from pacing API calls upfront to backing off when the provider tells you to wait.

API throttling vs. rate limiting: Who enforces, who adapts

Rate limiting and throttling both control how much traffic reaches an API, but they don’t handle excess requests the same way. A rate limit sets a cap on how many requests a client can make within a given period. Once you cross that cap, the provider can reject additional requests, often with a 429 Too Many Requests response.

Throttling can instead slow or delay requests when traffic exceeds an allowed rate. Either way, the provider controls the limit. As the API consumer, you control how your workflow responds: pacing requests to avoid the limit where possible and backing off when you hit it.

title: Why We're Moving n8n's Automation Team Beyond the Service Desk Model
content:
In the first article of our n8n on n8n series, Romina da Costa, our head of internal AI and automation, explains where the service desk model hits its limit. She also shares the four principles her team now follows to help every team at n8n build and own its automations.

What does success look like for an automation team? Workflows shipped, tickets closed, backlog cleared? TLDR: none of that is actually what makes an automation team successful.

Every centralized automation team solves a real business problem: automating routine tasks, freeing up time, and taking on work that doesn't actually need human judgment. But solving that well is exactly what lets the rest of the organization lean on you to keep solving it, instead of building that capability into how the organization actually functions. You're not fixing the bottleneck. You're shifting it downstream.

This isn't a mistake unique to n8n, and I don't think it's really a mistake at all. Most organizations, especially at the enterprise level, are going to arrive at some version of this same realization. You stand up a centralized automation team. You clear the backlog. You free people from routine work. All of that genuinely works, for a while. What you're left holding afterward is a problem nobody budgeted for: who actually maintains everything you just built, and whether the team that solved the first problem can carry the second one indefinitely.

title: Introducing n8n 3.0
content:
Today we're releasing n8n version 3.0.0 BETA

n8n 3.0 focuses on internal changes that improve reliability, stability and security, and lays the groundwork for the improvements we're building next. It clears out legacy features, tightens security defaults and reworks parts of how n8n runs under the hood.

The short version: the beta is available today and the stable release follows in early December. Because 3.0 includes breaking changes, some workflows and settings may need updates before you upgrade. The Migration Report in your instance tells you exactly which ones.

It’s worth taking a look now, even if you’re not planning to upgrade right away.

Why change the version number?

n8n follows semantic versioning. That means we don't ship breaking changes (updates that might require you to change your workflows or configuration) without bumping the major version number.

Over the past year we collected a list of breaking changes we wanted to make: legacy code paths to remove, defaults to make safer, a few features to retire. Each of them had to wait for a major version, so 3.0 brings them together in one release.

If you're wondering where the new features went, they didn't wait. We ship features continuously instead of saving them for a major version. Since 2.0 came out in December 2025, we've shipped over 45 releases, roughly one a week, and many of them included major new features. The full list is on our changelog.

That's why 3.0 can focus purely on the foundation, and everything new after the stable release ships on 3.x.

title: The Official Ruby SDK for MCP Reaches Tier 1
content:
The official Ruby SDK for Model Context Protocol is now a Tier 1 SDK, as defined in our SDK tiering system. Ruby is not alone here, and joins the company of our TypeScript, Python, C#, Go, and Rust SDKs.

When an SDK becomes Tier 1-compliant, it means that it reached the top of the three tiers, reserved for SDKs with the highest level of feature support, responsiveness to bugs and security issues, and alignment with MCP ecosystem priorities. If you build MCP servers or clients in Ruby, you can now sleep well knowing that you will get full spec feature support, a 100% conformance pass rate, support for new spec versions by their release date, issue triage within two business days, and critical bug fixes within seven days. This is especially important for developers that are responsible for production-grade services and applications, where being on the bleeding edge of MCP development is critical for the business.

Get the Ruby SDK → Read the documentation →

title: The New MCP Roadmap
content:
Today we’re excited to publish an updated roadmap for the Model Context Protocol (MCP), covering the next specification release and beyond.

It sets the direction for protocol work over the coming months and was developed by the Core Maintainers together with our community of maintainers and Working Groups.

Explore the roadmap →

Looking back

The previously published roadmap came out in March with four priority areas: transport evolution and scalability, agent communication, governance maturation, and enterprise readiness. We’ve made significant progress in all of these over the past five months.

The bulk of the changes landed in the 2026-07-28 specification release - you might’ve already seen them in our SDKs and documentation. The improvements ranged from minor modifications to major protocol overhauls.

One of the biggest changes we shipped is that protocol-level sessions and the initialization handshake are gone, so a server can scale horizontally without holding state (SEP-2575, SEP-2567). Additionally, clients can now call server/discover to learn a server’s supported versions and capabilities before doing anything else. List results are also cacheable (SEP-2549).

title: The 2026-07-28 Specification
content:
Since our last November release MCP continued to grow at an astonishing rate. Across our Tier 1 SDKs, we’re seeing close to half-a-billion downloads a month, with both TypeScript and Python SDKs crossing the 1 billion total downloads threshold. In just a few months, the protocol continued to grow as the data and interactivity substrate for agentic workflows.

Today, we’re officially pushing the release button on the next version of the MCP specification, 2026-07-28, along with the SDKs that will allow you to start building clients and servers right away.

The highlight of this release is a stateless protocol core - MCP is transforming from a bidirectional stateful protocol into a request/response stateless protocol. It was one of the most highly-requested features from developers who were eager to get better reliability and scalability for their MCP servers.

There is, of course, more to what we’re introducing with this version:

  • Every request is self-describing, with an optional discovery call for clients that want capabilities up front, so any request can land on any instance behind a plain round-robin load balancer.
  • Method and tool names travel in the Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name HTTP headers, so gateways can route and authorize on headers directly.
  • Server-to-client requests for things like sampling and elicitation are being redesigned to use Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR), removing the need for constantly open bidirectional streams.
  • List responses carry cache hints and a deterministic order, so clients can cache tool catalogs and keep upstream prompt caches stable across reconnects.

title: datasette-apps 0.3a0
content:
Release: datasette-apps 0.3a0

Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette.

These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent. This release improves that integration:

  • Apps can now be tagged in Datasette Agent chat messages by typing #, which autocompletes from the apps the user has permission to view.
  • New app_add_stored_queries() and app_remove_stored_queries() tools let the agent manage which stored queries an app is allowed to call. Granting a write query requires approval from the user first.
  • app_create() now checks that each requested stored query exists and that the user can view it, and asks the user to approve any write queries before the app is created.
  • The "View app" buttons shown by the agent tools, and the links on # app references, now open the app full screen in the Datasette Agent panel.

Tags: datasette, datasette-agent, datasette-apps

title: datasette-agent 0.5a0
content:
Release: datasette-agent 0.5a0

This is a significant release of Datasette Agent. The most notable new feature is called the panel - it lets the agent chat open and then sit next to pages from Datasette, for example a table or query page.

When combined with datasette-apps this means you can prompt a database-backed app into existence and then modify it from the chat that sits next to that app.

You can try it by signing in with your GitHub account to agent.datasette.io.

title: Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
content:
In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work.

Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO.

Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year.

We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended.

Watch the full conversation on YouTube →
